newsitem.title: UK: Competition fierce in quiet Europe grain market.
newsitem.headline: Competition fierce in quiet Europe grain market.

text.p: Competition among European grain traders remains cut throat, with too few buyers and fundamentally too much grain in a market which remains inactive in most areas.
Thursday's EU grain trader did little to improve the mood, traders said.
French wheat and barley prices slipped on Friday as operators focused on the low tonnages awarded by the EU, dealers said.
Poor export prospects inside and outside the EU also weighed on barley and wheat, they said.
The European Union awarded 211,350 tonnes of soft wheat with a refund of 18.99 Ecus per tonne, four Ecus more than the refund granted the previous week.
French exporters said the higher refund was good news but had been in line with expectations.
Instead they stressed that a weekly export award of 200,000 tonnes of wheat made it difficult for the EU to absorb its bumper crop.
French exporters said that the latest EU wheat award may help cover recent sales of French wheat to Tunisia and Iraq but was insufficient for business to Egypt.
They estimate that a EU wheat export refund of 20.00 Ecus per tonne was needed to cover sales to Egypt.
French wheat firmed earlier this week after Egypt bought 500,000 tonnes of French wheat, hitting a high of 857.50-860 francs per tonne in Rouen on Wednesday.
By Friday Rouen wheat was quoted at 855-857.50 francs per tonne, dealers said.
In internal EU business French wheat flows to the north of the European Union were slack despite a firmer British currency.
Business with Italy remained steady.
French wheat growers association AGPB said that between July 1, 1996 and January 8, 1997 French wheat sales to other European countries jumped 19 percent over the same period last year.
Barley prices eased five francs after the EU sharply reduced export volumes awarding only 26,000 tonnes of barley at a refund of 29.79 Ecus.
Industry sources linked the move to EU's concern over firm domestic prices and suspicion some exporters may be trying to corner the market.
In France exporters had bid for 220,000 tonnes exports at rebates ranging from 30.45 to 31.95 Ecus per tonne.
Rouen barley for February was quoted at 850 francs per tonne, down five on Thursday.
French maize prices were broadly unchanged after the European Union granted the import of lower than expected maize and sorghum tonnages to Spain at a reduced tariff in the first tender for 1997.
Fob Atlantic maize for March-April was unchanged from Thursday at 855-865 francs per tonne.
Exporters said they viewed the tender as a "testing ground", adding serious business would start next week.
News that the European Union rejected bids to import non-EU maize to Portugal may however benefit French maize exports, they said.
Exporters also said news France had a stronger than expected maize crop in 1996 may eventually weigh on prices in the face of slow demand.

France's grain office ONIC is expected to raise its estimate for the 1996 maize crop to 14.212 million tonnes from a previous target of 13.997 million tonnes and 12.394 million tonnes in 1995, industry sources said on Friday.
Slow sales at home and abroad are keeping German wheat prices under pressure, and the EU's tender did not provide enough encouragement to change things, traders said.
There are no buyers for bread wheat and domestic feed wheat offers are competing with Danish and British material, they said.
British feed wheat was reportedly sold at 263.50 marks per tonne cif north Germany, four marks below previous business.
News of the deal meant that consumers cut their bid levels for local feed wheat, with a knock-on effect on the local milling wheat market.
"There is still a lot of grain stored on farms which is looking for a market...this supply pressure will continue to depress prices," one broker said.
Brokers said more grain would now be offered into intervention than in the first three months of the Nov-May campaign, mostly feed rye, which was already leading.
British traders complained that sterling volatility was keeping the market uncertain. "If the pound goes the wrong way you're scuppered," one said.
For much of this week a combination of a strong pound and a strong market has precluded exports, although there are bits going to Germany and southern Europe, they said.
"We haven't seen a firm bid for large ports since the middle of December," one trader at one of the UK's leading companies said. "We just keep losing competitivity."
If there was to be a recovery in the level of activity on the UK market, it was not going to be export led, he said.

Danish wheat is still cheaper than British in Germany, British traders reckoned. But they were not surprised by German complaints about foreign competition "Their wheat is just too expensive," another British trader said.
Limited farm selling helps keep the market quiet. "If they don't get 90 stg ex-farm, they're not interested," one trader said. Farmers were not selling forward at all, he said.
Buyers are not short of spot supplies, traders said. "It's just a matter of waiting to see what happens," one said.
In Spain, trading in feed and milling wheat and barley was thin with ex-farm prices remaining largely unchanged, dealers said.
Durum wheat remained scarce reflected in high prices, but demand also dwindled.

Maize trading picked up as details of imports emerged. Dealers said, however, the EU's announcement on Thursday that it had authorised 56,000 tonnes of foreign maize to enter Spain did little to move prices.
"The market has already discounted these maize imports," one trader said.
Dealers said maize prices had slipped slightly as the maize harvest picked up again after being delayed by the rain.
Italian durum wheat prices were largely unchanged this week as internal demand continues to stagnate.
Dealers noted a pick-up in imports from the U.S, France, Syria and Australia.
Soft wheat prices eased on a fall demand for flour. Domestic demand tends to be slow in February and early March and then pick up as the Easter holidays approach, dealers said.
